ruling_text:
Huazano vs. Big K's Burgers, Inc. 1st C/A (breach of contract)

Anti SLAPP Motion
Motion for Limited Discovery

1. Anti-SLAPP Motion
The court GRANTS Defendant ABDULMAJID KARANOUH’s
special motion to strike the entire Complaint filed by
Plaintiff WAJIH MALKI pursuant to Section 425.16 of the
Code of Civil Procedure (the anti-SLAPP statute).

RJN: The court GRANTS Defendant’s unopposed request
for judicial notice of docket information for Malki v. Malki,
Case No. 25D004685. (Evid. Code § 452, subd. (d).)

Objections: The court SUSTAINS objections nos. 1 through
3 and OVERRULES objection no. 4 to the Declaration of
Wajih Malki.

The operative pleading is Plaintiff’s 6-page Complaint,
which purports to assert the following 11 causes of action
against Abdulmajid Karanough (the only named
defendant):

1. defamation (libel per se)
2. slander/republication
3. false light/invasion of privacy
4. intentional infliction of emotional distress
5. negligent infliction of emotional distress
6. interference with prospective economic advantage
7. civil harassment (Code of Civ. Proc., § 527.6)
8. civil extortion and coercion
9. injury to business reputation (Code of Civ. Proc., §
45)
10. fraud and deceptive misrepresentation
11. prima facie tort/malicious interference

Defendant moves to strike the Complaint in its entirety,
arguing that the claims arose from protective activity,
specifically a family law dissolution action involving Plaintiff
and Plaintiff's wife. Defendant here is the brother of
Plaintiff's estranged wife. (Compl., ¶ 6.)

The anti-SLAPP statute states: "A cause of action against a
person arising from any act of that person in furtherance of
the person's right of petition or free speech under the
United States Constitution or the California Constitution in
connection with a public issue shall be subject to a special
motion to strike, unless the court determines that the
plaintiff has established that there is a probability that the
plaintiff will prevail on the claim." (Code of Civ. Proc., §
425.16(b)(1).) The purpose of the anti-SLAPP statute is to
dismiss meritless lawsuits designed to chill the defendant's
free speech rights at the earliest stage of the case. (See
Wilcox v. Superior Court (1994) 27 Cal.App.4th 809, 815,
fn. 2, disapproved on another ground in Equilon Enterprises
v. Consumer Cause, Inc. (2002) 29 Cal.4th 53, 68.) The
statute is to "be construed broadly." (Code of Civ. Proc., §
425.16(a).)

An 'act in furtherance of a person's right of petition or free
speech under the United States or California Constitution
in connection with a public issue' includes: (1) any written
or oral statement or writing made before a legislative,
executive, or judicial proceeding, or any other official
proceeding authorized by law, (2) any written or oral
statement or writing made in connection with an issue
under consideration or review by a legislative, executive, or
judicial body, or any other official proceeding authorized
by law, (3) any written or oral statement or writing made in
a place open to the public or a public forum in connection
with an issue of public interest, or (4) any other conduct in
furtherance of the exercise of the constitutional right of
petition or the constitutional right of free speech in
connection with a public issue or an issue of public
interest.' (Code of Civ. Proc., § 425.16(e).)

To determine whether an anti-SLAPP motion should be
granted or denied, the trial court engages in a two-step
process. 'First, the court decides whether the defendant
has made a threshold showing that the challenged cause of
action is one arising from protected activity. The moving
defendant's burden is to demonstrate that the act or acts
of which the plaintiff complaints were taken "in furtherance
of the [defendant]' s right of petition or free speech under
the United States or California Constitution in connection
with a public issue," as defined in the statute. (Code of Civ.
Proc., § 425.16(b)(1).)' (Jarrow Formulas, Inc. v. LaMarche
(2003) 31 Cal.4th 728, 733.)
If that threshold is met, courts then look to the second
step, determining whether the plaintiff has demonstrated a
probability of prevailing on the merits. To do so, the
plaintiff must state and substantiate a legally sufficient
claim (Briggs v. Eden Council for Hope & Opportunity (1999)
19 Cal.4th 1106, 1122-1123), thereby demonstrating the
case has at least "minimal merit." (Cole v. Patricia A.
Meyer & Associates, APC (2012) 206 Cal.App.4th 1095,
1105.)
As noted above, there are four categories of protected
speech for an anti-SLAPP motion (Code Civ. Proc. §
425.16(e).) Here, Defendants argue that the conduct
alleged in the Complaint is protected under subdivisions
(e)(1) and (e)(2) of the Anti-SLAPP statute, which provide:
"(e) As used in this section, 'act in furtherance of a
person's right of petition or free speech under the
United States or California Constitution in connection
with a public issue' includes: (1) any written or oral
statement or writing made before a legislative,
executive, or judicial proceeding, or any other official
proceeding authorized by law, (2) any written or oral
statement or writing made in connection with an issue
under consideration or review by a legislative,
executive, or judicial body, or any other official
proceeding authorized by law ... ." (Code of Civ. Proc.,
425.16(e).
"The anti-SLAPP protection for petitioning activities applies
not only to the filing of lawsuits, but extends to conduct
that relates to such litigation, including statements made in
connection with or in preparation of litigation ... Indeed,
courts have adopted 'a fairly expansive view of what
constitutes litigation-related activities within the scope of
section 425.16."' (Kolar v. Donahue, McIntosh &
Hammerton (2006) 145 Cal.App.4th 1532, 1537 [Citations
omitted].)
"[J]ust as communications preparatory to or in anticipation
of the bringing of an action or other official proceeding are
within the protection of the litigation privilege of Civil Code
section 47, subdivision (b) [citation], ... such statements are
equally entitled to the benefits of section 425.16." (Briggs
v. Eden Council for Hope & Opportunity (1999) 19 Cal.4th
1106, 1115 [internal citations omitted]).
Importantly, the principal thrust or gravamen of a
plaintiff's cause of action determines whether the anti-
SLAPP statute applies. (Ramona Unified School Dist. V.
T siknas (2005) 135 Cal.App.4th 510, 519-520.)
Here, each of Plaintiff's claims appears to be primarily
based on the following allegations: In September of 2025,
"Defendant authored and distributed a letter to the law
firm representing Plaintiff's estranged spouse, containing
numerous false, malicious, and defamatory statements
about Plaintiff, including" accusations that
Plaintiff physically assaulted his wife in Jordan in
December 2024;
Plaintiff's wife was hospitalized as a result;
Plaintiff is mentally unstable, unfit, and dishonest;
"Plaintiff evaded taxes and could be subject to
imprisonment";
Plaintiff's businesses have collapsed and that only
one remains viable due to his wife's engagement";
and
Plaintiff attempted to abandon or 'dump' his
children on an incapable relative to safe money."
(Compl., 7.) The Complaint asserts these statements
were false or made with reckless disregard for the truth.
(Compl., 9.) Further, the Complaint alleges, in general
and conclusory fashion, that the communications were also
made to third parties in the United States, the Middle East
and Europe. (Compl., 10, 16.) The third parties are not
identified, nor are any dates provided. The Complaint then
generally references the statements in support of each
claim.
Defendant argues that the letter sent to the law firm
constitutes protected conduct. The court agrees.
Defendant submits his declaration wherein he attaches a
copy of an ex parte application that was provided to him by
the Bledsoe Law Firm (who Plaintiff contends is the firm
that is representing his spouse), in connection with the
Malki v. Malki matter. (Karanouh Decl., ¶ 2, Exh. B.) The ex
parte application was for an order “requesting no contact
with material uncle Abdulmajid Karanous and protection
from political/religious indoctrination.” (Karanouh Decl.,
Exh. B).
Defendant attaches a copy of the cover page of a letter
that he provided to the Bledsoe Law Firm in response to
the accusations. (Karanouh Decl., ¶ 3, Exh. C). This
document states, in part: “This document is for the sole
use of the Bledsoe Firm who is appointed by Myrna
Karanouh Malki to manage the legal affairs related to her
divorce from Wajih Malki. [¶] This document provides
evidence which totally contradicts and refutes the claim
made by Wajih Malki against Abdulmajid Karanouh, where
Wajih falsely accuses Abdulmajid of the following.... This
document includes a series of screenshots of WhatsApp
messages exchanged between Aji Malki...and his brotherin-law, Abdulmajid Karanouh, which support in refuting the
claims and accusations fabricated by Wajih against
Abdulmajid.” (Karanouh Decl., Exh. C). In sum, the letter
appears to be protected conduct.
The court finds that Defendant has made a threshold
showing that the gravamen and thrust of the Complaint is
based on protected activity. The court therefore proceeds
to the second step – to determine whether the plaintiff has
demonstrated a probability of prevailing on the merits.
The court finds that Plaintiff has not met that burden.
Plaintiff proffers only his own declaration in support of the
opposing papers. As Defendant notes, Plaintiff’s
declaration primarily relies on inadmissible hearsay.
(Again, the court sustains Defendant’s evidentiary
objections Nos. 1-3.) Plaintiff’s Declaration does state that
Defendant sent Plaintiff text messages on 8/7/25 accusing
Plaintiff of tax evasion and suggesting that such matters
would be publicly exposed. Such, however, is insufficient
to show that Plaintiff has a probability of prevailing on the
merits. By Plaintiff's own admission, "[t]hese text
messages are not offered as evidence of publication."
(Malki Decl., at p. 2, line 13.)
Accordingly, the motion is GRANTED.
In his opposing papers, Plaintiff alternatively requests leave
to amend. The request is denied.
As explained in Finato v. Keith A. Fink & Associates (2021)
68 Cal.App.5th 136, 149:
"[A] plaintiff whose complaint is stricken by a successful
anti-SLAPP motion cannot try again with an amended
complaint." (Dickinson v. Cosby (2017) 17 Cal.App.5th 655,
676, 225 Cal.Rptr.3d 430.) "Once the trial court has
determined the speech at issue is constitutionally
protected, it may not grant leave to amend to omit facts to
take the claim out of the protection of section 425.16."
(Mobile Medical Services, etc. v. Rajaram (2015) 241
Cal.App.4th 164, 171, 193 Cal.Rptr.3d 568.) Allowing an
amendment "once the court finds the prima facie showing
has been met would completely undermine the statute by
providing the pleader a ready escape from section 425.16's
quick dismissal remedy. Instead of having to show a
probability of success on the merits, the SLAPP plaintiff
would be able to go back to the drawing board with a
second opportunity to disguise the vexatious nature of the
suit through more artful pleading." (Simmons v. Allstate
Ins. Co. (2001) 92 Cal.App.4th 1068, 1073, 112 Cal.Rptr.2d
397 (Simmons).) Thus, "[t]here is no such thing as granting
an anti-SLAPP motion with leave to amend."
In light of the ruling, the court VACATES the scheduled
3/30/26 Case Management Conference.
Defendant to give notice.
2. Motion for Limited Discovery
The court DENIES Plaintiff WAJHI MALKI’s motion to open
limited discovery pursuant to Section 425.16(g) of the Code
of Civil Procedure.
Plaintiff seeks an order permitting limited, narrowly
tailored discovery to determine whether the letter at issue
in the Anti-SLAPP motion was intended for litigation, was
created in anticipation of a hearing, was meant to
influence a court, or was a private communication
unrelated to any judicial function. (Mov. Pts. & Auth. at p.
3, lines 9-15.)
At the same time, Plaintiff states he “can oppose the Anti-
SLAPP motion without discovery, but discovery will
materially assist the Court.” (Mov. Pts. & Auth. at p. 6,
lines 12-13.)
Good cause is not shown for the requested relief. As such,
the motion is DENIED.
Defendant to give notice.
